findings.name: shadcn/ui (CLI, registries, MCP server, skill)
findings.what_it_does: Copy-in React components (Base UI, React Aria or Radix, plus Tailwind) installed by a CLI and registries. Ships an MCP server and a Claude-readable skill. Since July 2026 'shadcn init' defaults to Base UI; '-b radix' selects Radix.
findings.how_we_use_it: Run 'shadcn init -t vite -b base', record the base in CLAUDE.md, then 'mcp init --client claude' and 'skills add shadcn/ui' so Claude installs canonical components. Theme with our tokens. Tell Claude to use the render prop, not asChild.
findings.last_activity: 2026-10-20 (GitHub API pushed_at, rechecked 21 Oct); CLI docs (-t vite, -b base|radix|aria) and the July 2026 changelog entry read 21 Oct
findings.saves: Canonical code from CLI and MCP means fewer fix-up loops and tokens; the default path keeps docs, skill and examples aligned.
findings.risks: Copied code becomes ours to maintain. Default look is generic without custom tokens. Base UI and Radix snippets differ (render vs asChild), so mixed examples break. Needs Node and pnpm, not installed yet.

findings.name: Base UI (new shadcn default) and Radix Primitives
findings.what_it_does: Unstyled accessible React components from the creators of Radix, Floating UI and MUI; MIT; npm @base-ui/react 1.9.0 (9 Oct 2026). Radix Primitives (WorkOS, MIT) stays supported and is used only when shadcn is initialised with -b radix.
findings.how_we_use_it: Consume through shadcn only; import directly just for custom widgets such as port popovers. Choose once and write it into PRODUCT.md and CLAUDE.md. Fall back to '-b radix' if a needed component is missing; shadcn's migration skill converts components later.
findings.maintainer: MUI and Base UI team (Radix: WorkOS)
findings.last_activity: Base UI pushed 2026-10-21, v1.9.0 on 2026-10-09; Radix primitives pushed 2026-10-14
findings.popularity: Base UI 11.2k stars, 298 open issues plus 133 PRs; Radix 19.4k stars
findings.saves: Focus, keyboard and ARIA behaviour for overlays and menus come prebuilt; following shadcn's default avoids doc and skill mismatches.
findings.risks: Younger than Radix, with fewer community snippets, so model habits (asChild) may mislead. Not tested here with our canvas popovers. React Flow UI registry items import no Radix directly (11 checked), so either base works.

findings.name: Tailwind CSS (v4, CSS-first)
findings.what_it_does: Utility-first CSS framework. Version 4 declares theme tokens as CSS variables in an @theme block instead of tailwind.config.js. Current npm release 4.3.3 (16 Jul 2026). shadcn and React Flow UI assume it.
findings.how_we_use_it: Tokens emit CSS custom properties that an '@theme inline' block references, so utilities follow theme switches. Light/dark via a data attribute on the root. Pin 4.3.x. Give Claude no tailwind.config.js guidance.
findings.saves: Compact class strings cost fewer tokens than bespoke CSS and keep generated UI consistent.
findings.risks: Long class lists hurt readability; token discipline needed. Data-attribute dark-mode syntax was not read (theme page only links it). React Flow's stylesheet must import after Tailwind.

findings.name: React Flow (xyflow)
findings.what_it_does: MIT library for node-based UIs: custom nodes, handles, edges, minimap. Docs: Tab focuses nodes and edges, Enter/Space selects, Escape clears, arrows move nodes. connectOnClick (default true) allows click-click wiring. No documented keyboard edge creation.
findings.how_we_use_it: Canvas engine, @xyflow/react 12.12.x, as a view over our own store. Set deleteKeyCode ['Delete','Backspace'], zoomOnDoubleClick false, panActivationKeyCode null. Typed ports via isValidConnection. We build keyboard 'Connect...' and an Edges list; dagre for Tidy; stop edge animation under reduced motion.
findings.last_activity: 2026-10-21 (GitHub API pushed_at; npm 12.12.0 on 2026-09-24); API reference, accessibility page and 12.12.0 stylesheet read 21 Oct
findings.saves: Avoids building pan/zoom, selection, wiring, minimap and focus plumbing from scratch.
findings.risks: Keyboard wiring is ours to build (WCAG 2.1.1). Default delete key is Backspace although ARIA text says 'delete'; Space both pans and selects. Its stylesheet animates edges with no reduced-motion rule. Large graphs need memoisation. Keep our graph JSON independent.

findings.name: React Flow UI (shadcn-based components; templates are Pro)
findings.what_it_does: Components for React Flow installed from a shadcn-style registry: base node, handles, status indicator, node search, zoom slider, devtools. Needs React 19 and Tailwind 4. Both templates are labelled Pro examples; Pro starts at $169 per month.
findings.how_we_use_it: Do not build on the templates. Read the component sources as references (11 checked import no Radix package, only React, @xyflow/react, lucide and shadcn parts). Vendor one only after xyflow confirms its licence; otherwise rewrite, since each file is short.
findings.license: Not stated per component; site footer links xyflow's MIT; registry files carry no licence header. Pro examples (templates, undo/redo) use the xyflow Pro License
findings.last_activity: Undo/redo example page updated 11 Oct 2026; component pages show no date
findings.saves: Study of finished, token-ready node, handle and status parts saves days of node-card design even if we rewrite them.
findings.risks: Component licence unresolved. Templates need paid Pro (Next.js, ELKjs, Zustand); the undo/redo example is also Pro-licensed, so build our own. Strict stylesheet import order. Newer, opinionated, few external references.

findings.name: cmdk (with kbar and React Aria fallbacks)
findings.what_it_does: Unstyled React command-menu component with filtering, keyword aliases and a dialog wrapper. shadcn's Command wraps it. npm 1.1.1 (14 Mar 2025) accepts React 18 or 19. Good to roughly 2-3k items.
findings.how_we_use_it: Ctrl/Cmd+K palette via shadcn Command, wrapped in our own Palette component so it can swap to kbar (timc1/kbar, MIT, npm 1.0.0, 10 Aug 2026) or React Aria's combobox (shadcn offers an aria base). Modules register commands, including 'Connect...'.
findings.saves: Fuzzy matching, keyboard handling and dialog wiring done; one CLI call to add.
findings.risks: Dormant: no release since March 2025, 76 open issues. React 19 is supported (earlier note was wrong). No virtualisation. Wrapping it keeps the swap cheap. React Aria is a second primitives set.

findings.name: react-resizable-panels (and dockview later)
findings.what_it_does: MIT React components for resizable, collapsible panel layouts with keyboard-friendly separators and layout save/restore. shadcn's Resizable wraps it. dockview (MIT core, 8.6.1 on 19 Oct 2026; enterprise package proprietary) adds tabbed docking.
findings.how_we_use_it: App shell: stage rail left, canvas centre, inspector and sources right. Collapse everything for Present mode and persist layout per stage. Keep dockview for later pop-out and tabbed docking.
findings.saves: Resizable, collapsible, persisted panels without custom drag code.
findings.risks: Single maintainer. API changed between versions. No tabbed docking or pop-outs; dockview is the upgrade but its enterprise package is proprietary.

findings.name: Claude design aids: Impeccable and Anthropic frontend-design
findings.what_it_does: Impeccable: design skill with 24 commands and 61 deterministic rules that flag AI-looking UI; its installer fetches an engine binary and writes hooks. Anthropic frontend-design: one short SKILL.md steering toward deliberate type, palette and one motion moment.
findings.how_we_use_it: Impeccable only after review (--no-hooks, DO_NOT_TRACK=1, inspect ~/.impeccable/bin), then critique and polish before demos after 13 Nov. frontend-design only for Present boards and landing pages, never the dense canvas. At most two design aids per session.
findings.license: Apache-2.0 (Impeccable); Apache-2.0 per-skill LICENSE.txt (frontend-design; repo root shows none)
findings.popularity: Impeccable 84.1k stars, 49 open issues; anthropics/skills 182k stars
findings.saves: Rule detection costs zero tokens; PRODUCT.md avoids restating the brief each session; frontend-design is cheap to load and trims aesthetic revisions.
findings.risks: Impeccable telemetry is on by default, its download host is unnamed, and hooks edit .claude/settings.local.json; it calls Inter overused. frontend-design targets marketing pages; repo licence field is empty, so rely on the per-skill Apache file.

findings.name: Vercel web-design-guidelines skill and Web Interface Guidelines
findings.what_it_does: A skill that reviews UI files against 100+ rules (visible focus, keyboard handlers, reduced motion, transform/opacity-only animation, undo for destructive actions) and prints terse file:line findings. Rules live in an MIT repo.
findings.how_we_use_it: Vendor a pinned copy of command.md into the project and run it on changed UI files before merges, instead of fetching main at review time. Add our canvas-specific rules beside it. It is the default review aid for the 13 Nov core.
findings.license: MIT (README; GitHub API shows no licence field for agent-skills)
findings.saves: Terse file:line output keeps review cost low; replaces writing our own checklist.
findings.risks: The skill fetches rules from GitHub main at run time (reproducibility, injection risk), so vendor and pin. Some rules are Next.js/Vercel-specific. Repo has no LICENSE file.

findings.name: IBM Carbon (design system and data-viz guidance)
findings.what_it_does: Apache-2.0 design system with concrete guidance for data-dense UI: data-viz palettes, chart anatomy, status indicators, notifications, empty states, light/dark tokens. Status pattern pairs colour with shape or symbol and text; warns that more than five or six indicators overwhelm.
findings.how_we_use_it: Reference, not a second component library. Borrow the status rules for Sourced / Team assumption / FALSE ASSUMPTION (colour plus icon plus word), notification persistence, categorical colour order, chart anatomy and empty-state structure.
findings.saves: Tested wording and rules for status, notifications and legends; no research from scratch.
findings.risks: Status page contradicts itself (three elements vs two) and sets no hard cap. Chart page says nothing on number formatting. Mixing Carbon components with shadcn gives two visual languages.

findings.name: Scientific colour maps (Crameri) and cmcrameri
findings.what_it_does: Perceptually uniform, colour-vision-deficiency-friendly maps that stay readable in black and white. Zenodo record 8.0.1 (5 Oct 2023, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.8409685) states the MIT licence. cmcrameri is the MIT Python wrapper.
findings.how_we_use_it: Default sequential and diverging ramps for sun, shadow, wind and energy. Export colour stops as JSON with the MIT notice; draw legends from the same stops; cite Crameri et al. 2020 and the DOI in the sources panel. Outline analysed surfaces; test ramp ends against the viewport in CI.
findings.saves: Avoids designing and testing colour ramps; citable for the sources panel.
findings.risks: JavaScript packaging not verified (66.9 MB zip). Categorical maps are limited. Only batlow, roma and vik checked, from a local data copy: none nears the FALSE magenta, but ramp ends fade into white or dark plates (1.1 to 1.7:1).

findings.name: Culori, Radix Colors and Style Dictionary (colour and token pipeline)
findings.what_it_does: Culori: MIT JavaScript colour library with OKLCH, interpolation and difference formulas. Radix Colors: MIT light/dark scales. Style Dictionary 5.7.0 (Apache-2.0, 16 Oct 2026): token build with first-class DTCG; the 2025.10 format is still partial.
findings.how_we_use_it: For 13 Nov, hand-written CSS variables with Culori scales from three inputs (base, accent, contrast) and contrast checks in CI; one-hour spike against Radix Colors, then pick one. In v1, DTCG JSON through Style Dictionary into the '@theme inline' block.
findings.maintainer: Evercoder (Dan Burzo); Radix (WorkOS); Style Dictionary org (DTCG: W3C community group)
findings.last_activity: Culori 2026-10-15 (npm 4.0.2); Style Dictionary npm release 2026-10-16; Radix Colors pushed 2025-12-17
findings.popularity: Culori 1.2k stars, 30 open issues; Style Dictionary 4.9k stars, 217 open issues; Radix Colors 1.7k stars
findings.saves: Programmatic palettes cut manual colour iteration and keep light/dark themes consistent; one token source stops Claude hard-coding colours.
findings.risks: Culori docs did not confirm gamut mapping or WCAG helpers; OKLCH lightness is no contrast guarantee. Style Dictionary adds a build step and 2025.10 gaps. Two palette sources in parallel would confuse; small communities.

findings.name: Observable (Plot, Framework and Runtime)
findings.what_it_does: Plot (ISC): layered-mark charts with colour, opacity and symbol legends and a standalone Plot.legend(). Framework and Runtime (ISC): reactive dataflow in which only blocks downstream of a change re-run and unobserved variables stay lazy.
findings.how_we_use_it: Plot for results panels and SVG board exports: one fixed-domain colour scale per metric, shared across compared options. Runtime and Framework are liveness references only (downstream-only recompute, lazy evaluation, invalidation), not dependencies. d3-scale-chromatic stays the fallback ramp source.
findings.license: ISC (Plot, Framework, Runtime); d3-scale-chromatic ISC plus Apache-2.0 ColorBrewer
findings.popularity: Plot 5.4k stars, 350 open issues; Framework 3.7k stars, 141 open; Runtime 1.1k stars, 2 open
findings.saves: Few lines per chart means fewer tokens than hand-written SVG or d3; the Runtime model gives a tested vocabulary for stale and lazy nodes.
findings.risks: Site docs returned HTTP 429; features read from repo docs and raw GitHub files. Plot has no 3D or radius and length legends. Framework is a static-site generator, not an embeddable engine. Last Plot npm release Feb 2025.

findings.name: Inter and Geist Mono typefaces
findings.what_it_does: OFL-1.1 fonts. Inter 4.1 (16 Nov 2024) is variable with an opsz axis that provides Display designs. Geist Mono lives in vercel/geist-font, whose fonts/GeistMono folder has variable and webfonts files. The npm geist package targets Next.js.
findings.how_we_use_it: Inter variable with opsz for UI and headings, tabular figures in tables and legends; Geist Mono for IDs, units, citations. Self-host files copied from the repos, with licence notices. Silence Impeccable's overused-font rule for Inter.
findings.popularity: Inter 20k stars; geist-font 3.7k stars, 53 open issues
findings.saves: Two free fonts settle type decisions early; tabular numerals make numeric panels readable.
findings.risks: Inter can read as generic. Geist files must come from the repo, not npm (Next peer dependency). Variable files need subsetting for load time. Geist Mono variable files were listed, not opened or rendered.

findings.name: Motion (motion.dev)
findings.what_it_does: MIT animation library for React, JS and Vue: springs, gestures, layout transitions. MotionConfig reducedMotion='user' disables transform and layout animation while keeping opacity and colour.
findings.how_we_use_it: Panel and phase transitions and node run-state pulses. Wrap the app in MotionConfig reducedMotion='user'. Tokens 100/200/300 ms, 400 ms only for large panel moves; ease-out entering, ease-in leaving; no bounce. Prefer CSS transitions for simple states.
findings.saves: Declarative variants reduce hand-written animation code and review tokens.
findings.risks: Layout animations on a big canvas can cost frames; test. MotionConfig does not cover CSS animations such as React Flow's animated edges. Motion+ paid tier is optional.

findings.name: Playwright MCP, Playwright CLI, Playwright Test and axe-core
findings.what_it_does: Playwright MCP (Apache-2.0) drives a browser via the accessibility tree. @playwright/cli is pre-1.0 (0.1.22, 28 Sep 2026). axe-core (MPL-2.0) finds about 57% of WCAG issues; @axe-core/playwright 4.14.0 runs it in tests.
findings.how_we_use_it: CI: Playwright Test (stable) plus @axe-core/playwright on shell, palette, panels and legends; fail on critical violations. Claude's interactive self-checks use the MCP or pinned CLI: tab through the canvas, screenshot phone and desktop widths, read console errors.
findings.popularity: Playwright MCP 38.4k stars; axe-core 7.7k stars, 444 open issues
findings.saves: Accessibility snapshots avoid vision tokens; axe catches many defects without LLM tokens.
findings.risks: MCP README says it is not a security boundary; one tool runs arbitrary JavaScript. CLI is pre-1.0. axe misses roughly 43% of issues and cannot inspect WebGL. Needs Node 18+, not installed.

findings.name: Rerun (viewer blueprint pattern)
findings.what_it_does: Apache-2.0/MIT multimodal data viewer. Docs: a blueprint is a layer separate from logged data; saved as .rbl files, shared, version-controlled; recordings sharing an Application ID share a blueprint; two resets (heuristic and default).
findings.how_we_use_it: Pattern only: store view layouts (panels, legends, camera, compared set) as shareable JSON apart from model data, keyed to the project. Offer 'auto layout' and 'reset to my default'. Community users fork layouts like modules.
findings.saves: Layout-versus-data separation avoids a later refactor of saved views.
findings.risks: Robotics-focused; its UI toolkit is not ours to reuse. Do not embed the viewer. 1,240 open issues.

findings.name: Speckle viewer (UX benchmark and speckle-server monorepo)
findings.what_it_does: Web viewer with dockable panels: Models, Filters, Views, Issues tabs, an Elements table dock, selection panel with 'add as filter', status-bar undo/redo, shortcut sheet. Saved views capture camera, filters, visibility, sections, measurements. Code: Apache-2.0 unless a folder says otherwise.
findings.how_we_use_it: Copy: Elements table (our 'View as table'), saved views as snapshots, panel shortcuts, layout lock/reset, colour-by-property. Viewer reuse (@speckle/viewer 2.31.14) is a roadmap candidate; coordinate with the viewer packet.
findings.license: Apache-2.0 by default; per-folder exceptions (GitHub shows NOASSERTION)
findings.saves: Reusing patterns, and maybe the viewer, could save weeks of three.js and panel design.
findings.risks: Mixed per-folder licences; Viewer 2 to 3 transition. Docs conflict on who may create views (Editor seat vs Contributor role) and list Views as 'soon'. Legends and themes unverified. Heavy stack.

findings.name: tldraw SDK and ComfyUI frontend (reference only)
findings.what_it_does: tldraw: infinite-canvas SDK, source-available; development free, production needs a licence key; starter kits MIT. ComfyUI frontend: GPL-3.0 node UI with node library, templates, subgraphs and App Mode; its litegraph.js base (MIT) is archived.
findings.how_we_use_it: Neither is a dependency. Read tldraw's MIT workflow starter kit for port-bound connections and click-output-to-pick-node, and ComfyUI's docs for templates, an App Mode-style linear view and a bookmarkable node library. Reimplement ideas on React Flow; copy no code.
findings.license: tldraw licence (source-available; GitHub reports NOASSERTION), starter kits MIT; ComfyUI frontend GPL-3.0
findings.popularity: tldraw 51k stars, 560 open issues; ComfyUI frontend about 2.1k stars, 3,056 open issues
findings.saves: Reading the starter kit and the docs saves usability iteration on node pickers and beginner on-ramps.
findings.risks: A public tldraw deployment counts as production and needs a key; coursework terms not found. Copying ComfyUI code would force GPL-3.0 onto ours. ComfyUI has 3,056 open issues and its docs omit node error states.

findings.name: WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation)
findings.what_it_does: Adds 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured, 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size (24 px). Understanding pages: 2.1.1 needs keyboard wiring, 1.1.1 chart alternatives, 1.4.1 colour never the sole cue, 2.2.2 pause, stop or hide for motion over five seconds.
findings.how_we_use_it: AA checklist: click-click wiring, keyboard 'Connect...' listbox, Edges list, 'View as table', 24 px ports, 3:1 for ports, wires and marks. Animated wires get a global 'Pause animations' control plus a reduced-motion rule; do not rely on the 'essential' exception.
findings.saves: Concrete pass/fail criteria prevent late accessibility rework.
findings.risks: Canvas and WebGL need custom semantics; automated tools cover part. Our 2.2.2 reading (users can interact during runs, so progress animation is probably not essential) is unaudited. Main page read in two chunks; Understanding pages read separately.

findings.name: deceptive.design and the gamification meta-analysis (Sailer and Homner 2020)
findings.what_it_does: deceptive.design lists 18 deceptive pattern types (nagging, fake urgency, confirmshaming, addictive design). Sailer and Homner pooled gamification studies in education: small positive effects, g=.49 cognitive, .36 motivational, .25 behavioural.
findings.how_we_use_it: PR checklist of the 18 types for notifications, counters, defaults and progress UI. Treat the ban on streaks and leaderboards as our values decision, not an evidence finding; allow only learning-supportive feedback (what-changed diffs, shortcut hints, attribution credit).
findings.maintainer: Harry Brignull (deceptive.design); Michael Sailer and Lisa Homner (Educational Psychology Review)
findings.license: deceptive.design not checked; the paper record is marked CC BY (Semantic Scholar)
findings.last_activity: deceptive.design unknown; paper online 2019, Educ Psychol Rev 32:77-112 (2020)
findings.saves: A ready taxonomy avoids debating each borderline UI choice; the meta-analysis gives a sourced counterweight to blanket anti-gamification claims.
findings.risks: deceptive.design is commerce-oriented. The meta-analysis covers classroom learning (k=9 to 19 per outcome); motivational and behavioural effects were less stable. Springer page needed a cookie redirect, so the abstract was read from Semantic Scholar's API.

findings.name: Autodesk Forma (compare and analysis UX benchmark)
findings.what_it_does: Commercial AEC site-design tool. Compare mode shows up to six proposals or analysis results side by side; zoom and pan sync; Inspect on one scene shows point details in every scene; 4K PNG capture. Navigator holds proposals and shared bases.
findings.how_we_use_it: Precedent for our Compare view: named snapshots, linked cameras, linked point inspection, context-sensitive right panel, saved camera views, 'variations as objects'. Cite it in the sources panel. Embodied-carbon page shows scenario data sources and editable values.
findings.saves: A ready, proven compare pattern avoids inventing one and testing it from scratch.
findings.risks: Closed source. autodesk.com tutorial pages return 403; read through a regional mirror and Autodesk blogs. Legends, units and uncertainty are not described in pages read. Unclear whether camera linking can be turned off.

findings.name: Figma UI3 and Linear redesign write-ups
findings.what_it_does: Figma UI3 (26 Jun 2024): canvas focus, collapsible panels, hide-all-UI; hover-only UI abandoned as unstable, some changes reverted for muscle memory. Linear (28 Mar 2024): LCH themes from three inputs instead of 98 variables, contrast setting, staged rollout.
findings.how_we_use_it: Template for the shell: stable panel positions, collapse-all for Present, optional labels, expert shortcuts untouched. Token generator from base, accent, contrast in OKLCH (Culori). Figma's named versions for option snapshots. Feature flags and staged rollout for UI changes after 13 Nov.
findings.last_activity: Figma article 2024-06-26; Linear article 2024-03-28; Figma version-history help page read 21 Oct 2026
findings.saves: Proven rationale for layout and theme choices; avoids repeating experiments Figma abandoned and hand-tuning dozens of colour variables.
findings.risks: Different audiences (product design, issue tracking). Linear's generator is unpublished, so ours is a reimplementation; no contrast measurements shown. Closed products; no screenshots reviewed. Figma rollout was gradual with no opt-in beta described.

findings.name: Spline (benchmark and community remix model)
findings.what_it_does: Browser-based 3D design tool with real-time collaboration and publishing. Its Community Platform lets users publish scenes, repost, comment and remix others' scenes; docs state community files are licensed CC BY 4.0.
findings.how_we_use_it: Benchmark for fork-and-remix: one-click remix of a module into your workspace, attribution preserved, licence shown on each item. Put a licence field in the module manifest. No Spline editor layout is copied.
findings.license: Commercial editor; community files CC BY 4.0 (docs)
findings.saves: Existing remix semantics and licence wording shorten community-feature design.
findings.risks: Editor open-source status unconfirmed (treated as closed). Interface-tour page not opened, so no editor UX claims. A search summary said CC0; the docs say CC BY 4.0. Pricing unchecked.

findings.name: Vancouver Tall Challenge page, terms and FAQ (Buildner)
findings.what_it_does: Panels are JPEGs up to 10 MB; the brief sets one to four. Judging is anonymous. FAQ: check AI tools' terms; AI images not advised as sole work. Dates: registration 29 Oct, questions 3 Nov, submission 30 Nov 2026.
findings.how_we_use_it: Derive the board export profile (JPEG, size cap, no identifying marks) and AI-image caption rules from these pages. Download the full brief yourselves and confirm panel count, size and AI wording before building Present mode.
findings.maintainer: Buildner with City of Vancouver and UBC SALA
findings.last_activity: Page re-read 21 Oct 2026: dates unchanged; lists dates to 26 Jan 2027 (results)
findings.saves: Early constraint knowledge prevents rework of the Present-mode exporter.
findings.risks: Brief PDF sits behind an email form (the Download brief link is a placeholder) that I did not submit, so A2, panel count and any AI rule are unconfirmed. Terms do not mention AI. Registration closes in eight days.

findings.name: Zustand with zundo, Yjs UndoManager and Immer patches (state and command layer)
findings.what_it_does: Three routes to one undoable store. zundo (MIT): temporal undo middleware for Zustand, which React Flow uses internally. Yjs (MIT): CRDT with Y.UndoManager scoped to tracked origins. Immer (MIT): patches and inverse patches.
findings.how_we_use_it: Half-day spike before canvas code: one command bus, React Flow as a view of the store. Pass test: drag, slider scrub and AI edit each undo as one labelled step; undo spans canvas, inspector and assumptions; named snapshots; deterministic JSON export. Record the choice in CLAUDE.md.
findings.maintainer: charkour (zundo); yjs org; pmndrs (Zustand); Immer (Michel Weststrate per docs copyright)
findings.license: MIT (zundo, Yjs, Zustand, Immer; per npm and GitHub pages)
findings.popularity: zundo 896 stars, 16 open issues; Yjs 23.0k stars, 118 open; Zustand 58.8k stars
findings.saves: One decided store avoids retrofitting undo, snapshots and autosave after 13 Nov and leaves a path to presence; zundo's README claims a footprint under 700 bytes.
findings.risks: zundo records every setter call unless equality or throttling is set and was last released Nov 2024. Yjs needs CRDT types rather than plain JSON. React 19 fit, README accuracy and 1,000-node performance untested; nothing spiked yet.

findings.name: Cognitive Dimensions of Notations (Green and Petre 1996; Green and Blackwell tutorial)
findings.what_it_does: Heuristic framework for judging notations and visual programming environments without costly studies. The tutorial (v1.2, 1998, 75 pages) defines 14 dimensions, including viscosity, hidden dependencies, premature commitment, secondary notation, progressive evaluation and visibility, and rates them per activity.
findings.how_we_use_it: Weekly walkthrough of the node-canvas contract: one row per dimension with the risk, the rule and a test task. Relays, auto-reconnection and frames map to hidden dependencies, error-proneness and secondary notation.
findings.license: Copyright 1998 Green and Blackwell; cite, do not copy
findings.last_activity: Tutorial v1.2, October 1998; Green and Petre in J. Visual Languages and Computing 7:131-174 (1996)
findings.saves: A ready checklist turns forum complaints into named design rules without a study; the tutorial's activity table shows which dimensions matter for modification and exploration.
findings.risks: A shared vocabulary, not a measurement; examples are 1990s (LabVIEW, Prograph). It rates hidden dependencies harmful for modification and exploration, our main activities. Green and Petre 1996 itself was read only through a review summary.

findings.name: Interruption and notification timing studies (Mark 2008; Iqbal and Bailey 2008)
findings.what_it_does: Mark et al. (48 people, email task): interrupted work finished faster at equal quality but with more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort. Iqbal and Bailey (16 users): notifications deferred to breakpoints caused less frustration than immediate delivery.
findings.how_we_use_it: Defer non-critical notices and community activity to breakpoints (save, stage switch, run finished while idle). Never interrupt a drag, wire or text edit. Let users set digest timing, since Mark found individual differences. Use as rationale, not proof for our tool.
findings.maintainer: Gloria Mark (UC Irvine); Shamsi Iqbal and Brian Bailey (UIUC)
findings.license: ACM CHI 2008 papers, author-hosted PDFs (cite, do not redistribute)
findings.saves: Replaces a Wikipedia flow citation with two primary studies that justify the notification rules cheaply.
findings.risks: Lab email, diagram-editing and programming tasks, not 3D analysis tools; papers are from 2008; Mark's sample was mostly German students. Iqbal's models recalled only 52-59% of breakpoints, with about 1.5 minutes average deferral.

findings.name: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (Amershi et al., CHI 2019; HAX Toolkit)
findings.what_it_does: 18 guidelines in four phases (initially, during interaction, when wrong, over time), refined through four phases including a study with 49 practitioners across 20 AI products. Full text is in the CHI paper and Microsoft's research blog.
findings.how_we_use_it: Map each AI feature to G1 and G2 (capabilities, quality), G3 (timing), G9 (efficient correction), G11 (why), G15 (granular feedback), G16 (consequences), G17 (global controls), G18 (change notices). Use as a review checklist beside the Vercel rules.
findings.license: ACM paper with Microsoft-hosted PDF; terms not checked (cite, do not copy)
findings.popularity: n/a (Honorable Mention at CHI 2019 per the Microsoft page)
findings.saves: Replaces a free-form AI-trust rule with numbered, citable guidelines; reviewers can cite G-numbers in PRs.
findings.risks: General and from 2019, before today's image generators. Participants found G11 often violated yet hard to supply. No legal weight; the HAX poster page was not needed once the paper text was readable.

findings.name: Execution-policy precedents: Grasshopper, Dynamo, Houdini and Honeybee
findings.what_it_does: Grasshopper: solver Enable, Disable, Toggle. Dynamo: Automatic, Manual, Periodic run modes saved per file. Houdini 22: Auto Update, On Mouse Up, Manual. Honeybee guide: save heavy run toggles as false so simulations never start on file open.
findings.how_we_use_it: Module manifests declare a cost class (live, interactive, batch). Live and interactive auto-run, sliders evaluating on release; batch waits for Run and shows stale. A global Auto-run lock like Grasshopper's solver; heavy runs never start on project open.
findings.maintainer: McNeel; Dynamo project; SideFX; Ladybug Tools
findings.last_activity: Houdini 22.0 docs; Dynamo page undated; McNeel Rhino 8 command page; Honeybee docs 'latest'
findings.saves: Proven user expectations for hold-back and re-run avoid inventing an execution model and testing it from scratch.
findings.risks: Sources differ in depth: Grasshopper from the McNeel command page plus a forum comment, Honeybee from one guide page. Defaults not tested by us; no study of what Grasshopper users expect. Thresholds are team assumptions.

principles.principle: Progressive disclosure, two levels at most, on a separate axis from workflow stage; the canvas is the hero. The brief's basic-advanced-present path mixes expertise with stage: a beginner can be in Evaluate while an expert is in Massing. Figma's UI3 write-up: canvas focus, collapsible panels, hide-all-UI; hover-only UI felt unstable and some moves were reverted to protect muscle memory. Linear cut navigation clutter without changing navigation behaviour. One ComfyUI commenter opposed a hide-nodes Beginner mode (single voice, thin evidence).
principles.rule_for_our_tool: Navigation rail = workflow stages (Massing, Program, Evaluate, Design, Present): persistent, free to jump because work loops back, each with an evidence-completeness indicator (inputs present, modules run, sources attached), never a score or a gate. Group them under the brief's Basic, Advanced and Present only if the 3-task test shows users do not read 'Advanced' as a gate. Essentials/Advanced is a separate per-module setting with a global default, one Advanced drawer deep, essentials on by default, everything searchable in the palette. Panels resizable and collapsible, layout remembered per stage; Present hides all panels by default; positions never move on hover; one inspector open. Document both axes in PRODUCT.md. Counts such as 'seven essentials' are team assumptions.

principles.principle: Protect flow with an explicit liveness model, tiered feedback, run states and fixable errors. Analysis cost varies by orders of magnitude, so one rule cannot serve a slider echo and a wind run. NN/g's limits (about 0.1 s instant, 1 s unbroken thought, 10 s needs progress and a way out) govern acknowledging an action, not delivering a result. Precedents: Grasshopper's solver lock; Dynamo's Automatic, Manual and Periodic modes saved per file, recalculating only changed nodes and downstream; Houdini's Auto Update, On Mouse Up and Manual; Honeybee's advice to save heavy toggles false; Observable's runtime, which recomputes only downstream and leaves unobserved variables lazy. Tanimoto's liveness levels (runnable diagram, edit-triggered updates, continuous) give vocabulary. The Cognitive Dimensions tutorial says novices, and anyone under interruption, need to check work-to-date at any time (progressive evaluation).
principles.rule_for_our_tool: Each module manifest declares a cost class (thresholds are team assumptions): live (under 100 ms), interactive (under 1 s), batch (longer). Live nodes auto-run; interactive nodes auto-run after a 300 ms debounce, and slider drags show a geometry proxy and evaluate on release; batch nodes run on demand and show 'stale' with a Run button. The 100 ms target applies to slider echo and proxy, never to results. A global 'Auto-run' lock (Grasshopper precedent), run mode saved with the project (Dynamo precedent); batch nodes never start on project open (Honeybee precedent). An upstream edit marks batch descendants 'stale (upstream)' and keeps their last result visible with a timestamp; cheap descendants recompute. Unobserved nodes stay lazy; Run all forces everything; step-in runs the chain up to the selected node. Nodes accept partial inputs and show placeholder warnings. States: idle, queued, running, stale, failed, warning, done, each icon plus word. Over 1 s show busy on the node; over 10 s show percent, ETA and Cancel; no modals or focus stealing. Errors name the cause and a fix; a refused wire drop says which type was expected. Memoise nodes, test onlyRenderVisibleElements; a node-count warning (start at 200) is a team assumption.

principles.principle: Wire density is the main readability problem, wire display is contested, and Cognitive Dimensions turns the complaints into a checklist. Informal coding of about 25 complaints across four threads: McNeel 48238 (16 posters), McNeel 55455 (23 posters on the page read), a Blender DevTalk UX proposal (18 posters on page one; only the opening post read) and a Hacker News thread (about 15 of 493 comments read). Themes: wire clutter, organisation at scale, surprising implicit behaviour, inconsistent conventions across tools, no text form to diff. In McNeel 48238 the Grasshopper author declined wire-display options for version 2 while at least three posters wanted faint or hidden wires, and four reported creating relays by accident through double-click. Blender's proposal objects to opaque auto-reconnection of occupied sockets. Green and Petre applied the framework to LabVIEW and Prograph: large visual programs were hard to comprehend, slow to modify and weak in secondary notation; the tutorial rates hidden dependencies harmful for modification and exploration, and says one-way or local links hide them. Signals only; Reddit stayed blocked.
principles.rule_for_our_tool: Wire modes Full, Faint and Selected-only, one click apart; selected node's wires always solid; default decided by the 3-task test. Weekly Cognitive Dimensions walkthrough of this contract: hidden dependencies, so selecting a relay highlights all partners with 'jump to', 'show dependents' works on any node or assumption, and the Edges list is two-way; viscosity, so replace-node-keeping-links, multi-select rewiring and dagre Tidy; premature commitment, so nodes can sit unconnected and be wired in any order; secondary notation, so frames, colour and notes never change meaning and live in layout JSON; progressive evaluation, so partial inputs run with placeholders; error-proneness, so no implicit reconnection (dropping on an occupied port previews and needs a modifier to replace) and relays need a modifier key, never a bare double-click; role-expressiveness, so ports carry colour, shape and label. Auto-created frames per module category with name and low-chroma tint. One documented shortcut map; set React Flow explicitly: deleteKeyCode ['Delete','Backspace'] (default is Backspace only), zoomOnDoubleClick false (double-click opens search), panActivationKeyCode null (Space also selects a focused node), shortcuts suspended inside text fields.

principles.principle: Inspect at the wire, preview live, and state units and precision. TouchDesigner docs describe animated wires, interactive node viewers and an info popup; Houdini docs describe flags, status badges and a node-info window. NIST's SI writing rules: a space between number and unit symbol, symbols never pluralised, no more significant digits than the measurement justifies. Carbon's chart pages cover tooltips and KPI numbers but not number formatting. Blender socket inspection remains unverified.
principles.rule_for_our_tool: Hover on any port shows value, type, unit, source module and last-run time; every output has 'pin to viewport'. Nodes show a thumbnail or sparkline, run time and warning badge; wire flow animates only during a run and can be paused. Every value carries an SI unit symbol after a space (for example 12.4 m, 310 kWh/m2). Default 3 significant figures with full precision on hover and copy (team assumption); never show more digits than the least certain input supports; unit conversions are explicit; the rounding policy per metric lives in the module manifest.

principles.principle: Onboard with templates, a linear App view, pulled help and useful empty states. NN/g found tutorials mostly forgotten and recommends help shown on user signal plus a persistent entry point. ComfyUI documents templates, App Mode and subgraphs as its on-ramp (docs re-read). Spline's community teaches by remixing others' scenes. Empty states need status, a learning cue and a direct action.
principles.rule_for_our_tool: By 13 Nov one starter graph on the real Vancouver block; by 10 Dec three (one per major stage group). An 'App view' (form plus results) over any graph. Help is pulled (hover '?', first-open hint) with one persistent Help/What's new entry; any tour (optional library Driver.js, MIT) is skippable, re-launchable and never hides focused items (WCAG 2.4.11). Every empty panel has a title, why it is empty, a primary action (import or load sample block) and a docs link; loading never renders as empty. Remixing a community module or graph is the learning route.

principles.principle: Keyboard-first command palette whose shortcuts teach. A good palette opens from anywhere, covers nearly every action, forgives typos, ranks by context and shows shortcuts. Speckle documents Shift+letter panel shortcuts and a cheat sheet; Forma offers a Quick access menu and zoom-to-fit shortcut. The ARIA pattern closest to a palette is an editable combobox with a listbox popup.
principles.rule_for_our_tool: Ctrl/Cmd+K toggles the palette and returns focus to its origin; it is the one shortcut that stays live inside text fields. Every action is a command (add node, toggle module, run all, switch stage, open sources, connect ports, export board) with fuzzy search, aliases, context ranking and visible shortcuts; aria-activedescendant on the input. A shortcut cheat sheet is reachable from the palette. The palette component is wrapped so cmdk can be swapped for kbar.

principles.principle: Explain every number, and keep status meanings from competing. PAIR: explain data sources, favour partial explanations with progressive disclosure, beware confidence displays that backfire. Forma's embodied-carbon analysis lets users view each scenario's data sources and customise them. Carbon's status pattern wants colour plus symbol or shape plus text and warns past five or six indicators. One node can carry seven run states, a warning and three evidence statuses, about ten semantic colours, so they must be split into channels. Midwest Uncertainty Collective work supports quantile dotplots and outcome plots, but evidence is limited, so test locally.
principles.rule_for_our_tool: Every metric opens 'Why this number?': formula, inputs, citation (title, link, retrieval date, section), status, editable value with diff from default, change history. Semantic palette (team assumption), three channels. (1) Evidence, the only status hues: Sourced blue #1D5FBF light / #7FB2FF dark, solid outline; Team assumption ochre #8A5A00 / #E3B341, dashed outline; FALSE ASSUMPTION magenta #B0126F / #FF7AC6, hatch, own icon, the words visible and in the accessible name. A node card shows one aggregate chip ('2 assumptions, 1 FALSE'); detail lives in the inspector. (2) Run state: icon plus word in the node header in neutral ink; only 'failed' takes a hue, deep red #6E0B0B / #FF6B5E; 'warning' is a neutral triangle, not amber, so it cannot be mistaken for ochre. (3) Data: Crameri ramps are the only large saturated areas; module categories use low-chroma tints plus names; the accent and two-tone focus ring avoid blue, ochre, magenta and red. Computed 21 Oct 2026: every token reaches at least 5.43:1 on four plates (failed 5.5:1); the light tokens have near-equal luminance (0.108 to 0.127), so greyscale prints cannot tell them apart and boards add patterns and words. Colour-vision simulation (Machado 2009 matrices, severity 1.0, CIELAB dE76; it reproduces the reviewer's blue-magenta drop from 66 to 32): Sourced versus FALSE falls to 32 for protan (light) and 17 (dark); a first-draft red #B42318 against ochre fell to 2.2 for deutan, so failed was darkened (minimum 25 against ochre). Pairs under about 20 never rely on hue alone (team threshold). FALSE stays at least 47 dE from batlow, roma and vik; Sourced and Team come within 8 to 9 of parts of roma, so chips sit on opaque plates. Superseded values use <del> plus the word 'superseded': JAWS, Narrator and macOS VoiceOver do not announce <s> by default (NVDA says 'deleted'); no strikethrough on explanatory text. Where a result depends on editable assumptions, show a range band or quantile dots naming the drivers; pilot with 3-5 classmates. Chip cap per screen is an editable team assumption. Flagged claims stay visible.

principles.principle: Make work reversible, and decide the state layer first. NN/g lists undo and redo under user control. Figma autosaves checkpoints (every 30 minutes), lets users name versions, and restores without deleting anything. Speckle puts undo/redo in its status bar and saves views with camera, filters and sections. Rerun keeps layout apart from data and offers two reset levels. FME wires a visual Compare tool into git diff and merge; about three HN voices say visual programs are hard to diff or give to AI without a text form. Undo across canvas, inspector, palette and AI edits only works if every action passes through one store. React Flow already runs on Zustand and its docs use Zustand for app state; its undo/redo example is Pro-licensed. Options: zundo (MIT, temporal middleware; each setter call is a history entry unless equality or throttling is set), Yjs UndoManager (MIT; merges edits within 500 ms by default, scopes undo to tracked origins, stopCapturing splits steps; needs CRDT types), Immer patches and inverse patches (MIT; usable for undo and for syncing).
principles.rule_for_our_tool: One command bus: every user action (palette, shortcut, drag, scrub, AI edit) is a serialisable, named command applied to one store; React Flow is a view of it, not the source of truth. Half-day spike before canvas code with acceptance tests: a node drag, a slider scrub and an AI edit each undo as one labelled step; undo spans canvas, inspector and assumption edits; 'Save option' makes a named snapshot; export is deterministic key-sorted JSON; a 1,000-node graph stays responsive. Default pending the spike: Zustand with zundo (smallest step); move to Yjs only if live collaboration is wanted before 10 Dec. Continuous autosave; restore adds a checkpoint and deletes nothing; forks open a visual graph diff (planned after 10 Dec). Layouts and views are separate JSON from model data, with 'auto layout' and 'reset to my default'.

principles.principle: Compare options side by side, with linked views. Autodesk Forma's Compare mode shows up to six proposals or analysis results, syncs zoom and pan, and echoes point inspection in every pane (Autodesk quick-start page, opened via a regional mirror). NN/g comparison guidance: about five items, aligned attributes, sticky headers, highlight differences, hide identical attributes.
principles.rule_for_our_tool: Compare view of named snapshots: one pane or column per option (up to six, compact layout above four; both numbers are editable guidance), aligned metric rows, sticky headers, 'show differences only', shared legends and scales, linked camera and linked point inspection on by default with an off switch (Forma precedent; whether Forma has a toggle is unverified), and PNG export of the compared view.

principles.principle: Colour scales and legends must read at a glance, and no background can carry a whole ramp. Use perceptually uniform, colour-vision-safe maps (Crameri, MIT per Zenodo); separate sequential from diverging by data meaning; label directly where possible. Colour must not be the only cue (WCAG 1.4.1) and graphics need 3:1 contrast (1.4.11). Carbon: legends explain each visual property, and a data table is the only route to very small slices. Observable Plot draws ramps for continuous scales and swatches for ordinal or threshold scales. Computed from a local 256-step copy of batlow, roma and vik: batlow's light end #FACCFA is 1.4:1 on white and its dark end #011959 is 1.1:1 on #16181C; against mid-grey #8A8D91 each ramp passes through about 1:1 somewhere along its length, so every lightness-ordered ramp crosses the background's lightness.
principles.rule_for_our_tool: Crameri-style sequential maps by default; a diverging map only when data has a meaningful midpoint; no rainbow; no shipped ramp ends in the FALSE ASSUMPTION hue. Legend always visible on the canvas with units and threshold ticks, drawn from the same colour stops as the shading, with outlined swatches. Compared options share one scale. Do not rely on the viewport background for contrast: give analysed surfaces a 1 px neutral edge, keep context and ground in neutral greys, add patterns, labels or values beside colour, and check ramp ends against each theme's viewport in CI with Culori. Every analysis offers 'View as table'.

principles.principle: Notification restraint and ethical engagement, with evidence. Mark et al. (CHI 2008, 48 participants, lab email task): interrupted tasks were finished faster at equal quality, at the price of more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort; interruption context made no difference; openness to experience and need for personal structure predicted disruption cost. Iqbal and Bailey (CHI 2008, 16 users): notifications deferred to breakpoints caused less frustration than immediate delivery, at about 1.5 minutes average deferral; in diagram editing, medium breakpoints beat fine ones and immediate delivery; relevant content was tolerated better. Amershi G3: time services based on context. NN/g and Carbon: match interruption to urgency; never time out critical messages. deceptive.design lists 18 patterns. Sailer and Homner (2020) found small positive effects of gamification on learning (g=.49 cognitive, .36 motivational, .25 behavioural; cognitive stable, others less so; game fiction and competition combined with collaboration helped behaviour), in classrooms, not professional tools.
principles.rule_for_our_tool: No toasts by default; status inline on the node. Never interrupt a drag, wire, text edit or open popover. Non-critical notices (community activity, module updates, what's new) wait for a breakpoint (save, stage switch, run finished while idle); critical errors appear inline at once without stealing focus; users set digest timing. Toasts only for non-critical events and auto-dismiss only without an action. No streaks, points, leaderboards, fake urgency or social proof, confirmshaming or nagging: a values decision, since game elements can help learning. Allowed, learning-supportive feedback: a 'what changed' diff after each run (Amershi G16), progressive shortcut hints, evidence completeness per stage, attribution credit on forks. Community notifications and analytics opt-in. Never optimise time-in-app; success is a task completed with fewer errors.

principles.principle: Tokens, themes, type and motion from small sets. Linear generates themes in LCH from three variables (base, accent, contrast), replacing 98 variables. OKLCH keeps lightness consistent but guarantees no contrast. NN/g: light mode generally reads better; offer dark as a user choice. NN/g animation: about 100-400 ms, around 100 ms for simple feedback, 200-300 ms for larger changes, 400 ms only for large moves; ease-out entering, ease-in exiting; parallax only with caution; honour reduced motion. Motion's MotionConfig covers its own animations only: React Flow's stylesheet animates animated edges with a 0.5 s dash loop and has no reduced-motion rule (12.12.0, read 21 Oct). Tailwind 4 reads tokens from CSS variables. Inter 4.1 has an opsz axis for Display sizes.
principles.rule_for_our_tool: Tokens are CSS variables for 13 Nov, DTCG JSON through Style Dictionary v5 later. Neutral, accent and status scales come from three inputs in OKLCH plus a contrast control; light, dark and high-contrast by user choice; chrome low-chroma so analysis colours are the only saturated hues; viewport background themed separately. Durations 100, 200, 300 ms, 400 ms only for large panel moves; ease-out in, ease-in out; animate transform and opacity only; no bounce; no parallax (team decision). MotionConfig reducedMotion='user' plus a CSS prefers-reduced-motion block that stops edge dash animation, and a global 'Pause animations' switch; running falls back to a static icon. Inter variable with opsz plus Geist Mono, tabular figures, five type sizes.

principles.principle: WCAG 2.2 AA is reachable in a canvas tool only if wiring, motion and viewport results get non-pointer and non-visual routes. React Flow documents Tab focus, Enter/Space selection, Escape, arrow-key moves and an assertive live region, but not keyboard edge creation; its default ARIA text says press delete while deleteKeyCode defaults to Backspace. WCAG 2.1.1's Understanding page says connect-the-dots tasks need keyboard operation; 2.5.7 is met by click-click (connectOnClick). Precedents: IBM App Connect Toolkit's dialog with source and target terminal lists, Foblex f-flow v19 (C, arrows, Enter), Blender's Make Links (J). 1.1.1: charts need short plus long alternatives and tables are recommended; Speckle's Elements dock is precedent. 2.2.2 (Level A): moving content that starts automatically, lasts over five seconds and sits beside other content needs pause, stop or hide unless essential; a loading animation is essential only when users cannot interact, and users can interact during a run.
principles.rule_for_our_tool: A 'Connect...' command on each focused port (also in Ctrl+K) opens a listbox of type-compatible target ports with type-ahead; an Edges list in the inspector with delete and rewire; click-click wiring and numeric inputs beside sliders; 24 px port hit areas or spacing; scroll-padding so panels never hide focus; 3:1 for ports, wires, focus rings and chart marks; 'View as table' (values per facade or zone) plus a long text summary for each viewport analysis. Animated wires: global 'Pause animations' control, reduced-motion CSS, static 'running' icon fallback; do not lean on the essential exception. React Flow keyboard features on; axe-core in CI plus a manual keyboard and screen-reader pass.

principles.principle: Design Present mode around the competition's real constraints and the pixels AI renders actually have. Buildner terms: each panel is a JPEG of at most 10 MB, the brief sets one to four panels, judging is anonymous and marks that identify entrants are banned; the FAQ tells entrants to check AI tools' terms and not to treat AI images as sole work. The terms do not mention AI. A2 is 420 x 594 mm (4961 x 7016 px, 34.8 MP, at 300 dpi, computed). OpenAI's image guide (read in full 21 Oct) allows up to 3840 px per edge, 655,360 to 8,294,400 px, multiples of 16, aspect 1:3 to 3:1, and calls sizes above 2560 x 1440 experimental; it names gpt-image-2.5 variants. A full-sheet A-ratio render at the cap (2416 x 3432) is about 146 dpi on A2; 150 dpi would need 8.7 MP. Poster-type guidance comes from scientific-poster guides (UAB: 32 pt body on 36 x 48 in).
principles.rule_for_our_tool: Board template on a 12-column grid (team assumption). Export profile: sRGB JPEG per panel; start at 300 dpi and step quality, then dpi, down until under 10 MB, showing the resulting size; strip identifying metadata. Type: body default 14 pt (UAB's 32 pt scaled by about 0.49 to A2), floors 10 pt body and 8 pt legends (team assumptions); preview at fit-to-screen (about 1080 px tall). Charts are vector, rasterised at export, with units. AI renders: show effective dpi on the board (a 2560 px render at full A2 width is about 155 dpi), warn under 150 dpi (team assumption), size hero images to the pixels available and caption any upscaling ('AI-assisted, upscaled'). Every AI image gets a visible caption 'AI-assisted image' with model and date; the project logs prompt, exact model ID and size requested, since stripped metadata cannot carry provenance. Confirm the brief's AI wording first. Boards link to live model values and show a 'stale' badge after upstream edits.

principles.principle: Treat AI output as a labelled draft with provenance and a human in the loop, using Amershi et al.'s numbered guidelines (CHI 2019: 18 guidelines in four phases, from a study with 49 practitioners across 20 AI products). Buildner's FAQ warns that AI-generated images may not be the entrant's sole IP. PAIR: explain data sources, show partial explanations, prompt verification in high-stakes low-confidence cases, show alternatives. In the paper's study, G11 (make clear why the system did what it did) was among the most often violated, though participants could imagine explanations in most products.
principles.rule_for_our_tool: Map AI features to the guidelines. G1 and G2: say what the AI can do and how often it errs. G3: deliver at breakpoints. G9: every AI action is editable and undoable in one step. G11: AI-generated text, values and images carry an 'AI draft' label and show inputs and sources. G15: granular feedback on each suggestion. G16: show the consequence of accepting (what changes downstream). G17: a global off switch. G18: a change note when the model or version changes. AI-suggested thresholds enter as Team assumption until a person attaches a source; never as Sourced. Show model name and version, keep prompts, offer two or more alternatives for generated images, and never auto-apply AI edits to the graph.

recommendations.decision: Build the shell on Vite, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind 4.3 (CSS-first), shadcn ('init -t vite -b base') and MIT @xyflow/react 12.12 with our own node cards. Install Node LTS and pnpm first. Before any canvas code, run a half-day state spike (Zustand with zundo, Yjs UndoManager, Immer patches) and record the one command bus in CLAUDE.md; React Flow stays a view of that store. Do not depend on React Flow UI templates or its Pro undo/redo example; vendor a React Flow UI component only after xyflow confirms its licence, otherwise rewrite it.
recommendations.rationale: shadcn's CLI docs list -t vite and -b base|radix|aria, and its July 2026 changelog makes Base UI the init default (read 21 Oct). The 11 React Flow UI registry files checked import no Radix package. Both templates and the undo/redo example are Pro. Undo across canvas, inspector, palette and AI edits, plus snapshots, autosave and later presence, depends on one store decided up front; retrofitting after 13 Nov is the classic rewrite. React Flow already uses Zustand and documents it for app state, so zundo is the smallest step; Yjs buys presence later. Record the base in CLAUDE.md and PRODUCT.md, tell Claude to use 'render' not 'asChild', pin versions.
recommendations.alternatives_rejected: '-b radix' as default (kept as fallback); Pro templates and the Pro undo example; tldraw (production licence key); ComfyUI frontend and litegraph (GPL-3.0, archived); Rete.js (README showed no plugin detail); Blueprint or Carbon React (second visual system); choosing the state layer after the canvas exists.

recommendations.decision: Keep Claude's design aids minimal: always the shadcn skill and MCP, plus one of the vendored Vercel checklist (default for 13 Nov) or Impeccable (after review, from 14 Nov). Use Anthropic's frontend-design only for Present-mode and landing pages. Do not install UI UX Pro Max. At most two aids per session. Use Amershi's numbered guidelines as a human review checklist for AI features, not as another skill.
recommendations.rationale: Five aids at once work against the token-saving goal and overlap context. Impeccable downloads an engine binary into ~/.impeccable/bin, writes hooks into .claude/settings.local.json that can trigger that download even if the launcher is denied, sends anonymous telemetry unless disabled, and its README lists Inter as overused. Review it with --no-hooks and DO_NOT_TRACK=1 first. Vercel's skill fetches rules from GitHub main, so vendor a pinned copy.
recommendations.alternatives_rejected: Installing every design skill together; unpinned Vercel fetch; Impeccable hooks on by default; UI UX Pro Max (MIT, 79 styles; overlaps and adds context, so dropped as a finding); Playwright MCP as the default review tool.

recommendations.decision: Make the journey a persistent five-stage rail (Massing, Program, Evaluate, Design, Present), free to jump, each stage with an evidence-completeness indicator. Keep Essentials/Advanced as a separate per-module disclosure setting. Group the stages under the brief's Basic, Advanced and Present labels only if the 3-task test shows users do not read 'Advanced' as a gate. Adopt an engagement-ethics policy: no streaks, points, leaderboards, fake urgency or social proof, nagging or confirmshaming; opt-in digests; inline status; non-critical notices wait for breakpoints.
recommendations.rationale: The brief's basic-advanced-present path mixes expertise with workflow stage: a beginner can be in Evaluate while an expert is in Massing, so a rail cannot show where the user is. NN/g supports two-level progressive disclosure and staged flows only for independent steps; our stages loop back. Figma and Linear keep focus on the canvas and avoid hover-only UI. deceptive.design gives 18 named patterns; Sailer and Homner find small positive classroom effects (g .25 to .49), so the leaderboard ban is a values decision. Mark and Iqbal and Bailey support deferring non-critical notices.
recommendations.alternatives_rejected: A locked wizard; expertise tiers as the main navigation; a Beginner mode that hides nodes (one ComfyUI commenter objected; evidence thin, so test before building); badges and XP for module uploads; countdown banners; push-style tours.

recommendations.decision: Write the node-canvas contract with an execution policy: each module declares a cost class (live, interactive, batch); live and interactive nodes auto-run, batch nodes wait for Run and show stale; a global Auto-run lock; no batch run on project open. Add typed ports, three wire modes, relays by modifier key, no implicit reconnection, hover inspection with units, click-click wiring, keyboard Connect, an Edges list and explicit React Flow shortcut defaults. Review the contract weekly against the Cognitive Dimensions.
recommendations.rationale: Without a liveness model, the 100 ms preview, stale propagation and Grasshopper's auto-solve habit conflict: NN/g's limits cover acknowledgement, not wind or energy results. Grasshopper, Dynamo, Houdini and Honeybee all let users hold back heavy runs; Observable recomputes only downstream and lazily. Wire clutter and implicit behaviour recur across McNeel, Blender, Hacker News and Unreal sources (informal coding of about 25 items), and the Cognitive Dimensions tutorial rates hidden dependencies harmful for modification and exploration. WCAG 2.1.1 and 2.5.7 need keyboard and non-drag routes; React Flow documents neither keyboard edge creation nor a Delete key default.
recommendations.alternatives_rejected: Auto-run everything; manual-run everything; free-form wiring without categories; drag-only connection; elkjs from day one (large); relying on React Flow's keyboard support alone; hiding wires by default (the McNeel thread is split); double-click relays.

recommendations.decision: Build one reusable SourceChip and 'Why this number?' panel with three statuses (Sourced, Team assumption, FALSE ASSUMPTION), each always icon plus word, inside a three-channel semantic palette: evidence hues; run state as neutral icon plus word with a hue only for failed; data ramps. Node cards show one aggregate evidence chip. AI-suggested values enter as Team assumption until a person attaches a source.
recommendations.rationale: PAIR advises explaining sources and favouring partial explanations; Carbon pairs colour with symbol and text and cautions past five or six indicators; WCAG 1.4.1 forbids colour-only meaning; Forma's embodied-carbon analysis already exposes editable scenario sources. About ten semantic colours on one card would exceed Carbon's caution, so the channels are split. Colour-vision simulation shows hue alone fails for several pairs (dE76 17 to 32), so shape and words carry the meaning; contrast is at least 5.43:1 on four plates.
recommendations.alternatives_rejected: Footnote-only citations; colour-only flags; per-value chips on every node; amber for warning (collides with Team assumption ochre); a red-family failed hue at the first-draft value (2.2 against ochre for deutan); hiding falsified claims (the brief requires they stay visible); strikethrough on explanations.

recommendations.decision: Create the token system in steps: CSS variables with Culori OKLCH scales for 13 Nov; DTCG JSON with Style Dictionary v5 later; Inter 4.1 (opsz) plus Geist Mono self-hosted from their repos; Crameri maps (MIT) for analysis colour on outlined surfaces; low-chroma chrome; Radix Colors only as a one-hour comparison.
recommendations.rationale: Linear shows three inputs can generate a whole theme; OKLCH gives consistent lightness; Crameri maps are uniform and colour-vision friendly, and Zenodo states MIT. Style Dictionary v5.7 supports DTCG but not fully the 2025.10 format. Tailwind 4 consumes CSS variables via '@theme inline'. No background carries a whole ramp (computed on batlow, roma, vik), so edges and legends do the work. Reserving saturation for data keeps results readable.
recommendations.alternatives_rejected: Hand-picked hex values; rainbow colour maps; Radix Colors and Culori in parallel; dark-only default; npm geist package (Next.js peer dependency); a tailwind.config.js theme; relying on a themed viewport background for ramp contrast.

recommendations.decision: Standardise results and options: Observable Plot with shared scales and always-visible legends, uncertainty bands where assumptions are editable, named option snapshots with global undo, a Compare view for up to six options with linked camera and linked point inspection, and 'View as table' for every analysis.
recommendations.rationale: Forma documents up to six compared results, synced views and inspect-in-all-panes; NN/g gives comparison rules; Carbon gives chart-anatomy rules; Figma and Speckle show snapshot and saved-view models; Plot's repo docs confirm legends from a scale definition. Snapshots are a prerequisite of Compare.
recommendations.alternatives_rejected: Single-number KPIs without ranges; per-chart auto-scaling that breaks cross-option comparison; hand-written SVG charts; a compare view without snapshots.

recommendations.decision: Make Present mode follow the competition: JPEG export profile under 10 MB per panel, anonymity-safe metadata, visible AI-image captions with a prompt and model log, effective-dpi readout with an upscaling disclosure, and live-linked board values. Download the full brief yourselves and confirm panel count, A2 and AI wording; email organisers before the 3 Nov question deadline; registration closes 29 Oct.
recommendations.rationale: The Buildner terms set JPEG, 10 MB and anonymity, and the FAQ points to AI-tool terms; the brief PDF sits behind an email form that I did not submit. Stripping metadata for anonymity removes any embedded provenance, so provenance must live in captions and logs (the image guide says nothing on C2PA). An A2 sheet at 300 dpi is 34.8 MP while the image model tops out at 8.3 MP, so full-sheet renders land near 146 dpi. Type sizes are scaled from a scientific-poster guide and are team assumptions.
recommendations.alternatives_rejected: Exporting 300 dpi PNG; relying on C2PA metadata for provenance (OpenAI's claim not found in the guide); assuming four A2 panels; leaving AI images unlabelled; stretching renders to fill the sheet silently.

recommendations.decision: Set quality gates: WCAG 2.2 AA, Playwright Test plus @axe-core/playwright in CI (pinned), the vendored Vercel checklist on changed UI files, Playwright MCP or pinned CLI for Claude's self-checks. Before 13 Nov run five 30-minute think-aloud sessions with Grasshopper-using classmates plus a 3-task test of the stage rail and node card, recording task success, time on task, errors and wrong turns, raw NASA-TLX, UMUX-Lite and a flow short scale; repeat the same tasks after 13 Nov. Judge by behaviour, not looks. Never optimise time-in-app.
recommendations.rationale: axe-core finds about 57% of WCAG issues. The aesthetic-usability effect (Kurosu and Kashimura 1995, per NN/g) means attractive UIs are rated easier than they are, so compare what participants do with what they say. Mark et al. used a modified NASA-TLX with a stress item; UMUX-Lite is two items and tracks SUS (r about .83 per MeasuringU's summary); the flow short scale exists in 10-item and 16-item forms, so pick one and keep it. Five sessions give descriptive trends, not statistics. Forum evidence gathered so far is informal.
recommendations.alternatives_rejected: Visual taste checks only; relying on Impeccable's detector alone (it targets AI-looking design, not WCAG); unpinned pre-1.0 @playwright/cli; engagement metrics such as time in app or return frequency.

recommendations.decision: Sequence the UI work. First week: state-layer spike and command-bus decision. By 13 Nov: shell and panels, CSS-variable tokens, canvas with typed ports and module cost classes, palette, one starter graph, SourceChip and 'Why this number?' panel, keyboard Connect, global undo. By 10 Dec: Compare with snapshots, uncertainty displays, table views, three starter graphs, motion, Present export profile with dpi readout, onboarding hints, CI accessibility, polish pass. Later: dockview, graph diff for forks, community theme tokens and module licence field, Yjs-based presence and comment pins, Speckle viewer extensions.
recommendations.rationale: Core items directly serve the module canvas, evidence and focus goals; polish and onboarding extras depend on stable components. Global undo and snapshots are only feasible by 13 Nov if the state layer is decided first, and Node is not installed yet. Dates are the course deadlines supplied in the brief. Optional half-day parameter-panel spike (Leva or Tweakpane) in the v1 window.
recommendations.alternatives_rejected: Starting with Present-mode boards; building docking or community theming before the core canvas works; shipping all three starter graphs for 13 Nov; coding the canvas before the state layer is chosen.

flags.detail: React Flow's accessibility and API docs (read 21 Oct 2026) describe Tab focus, Enter/Space selection, arrow-key node movement and edge deletion; connectOnClick (default true) covers single-pointer use (2.5.7). Neither documents creating edges from the keyboard. WCAG 2.1.1's Understanding page says connect-the-dots tasks, where only endpoints matter, need keyboard operation.
flags.correction: Build a keyboard 'Connect...' command with a type-compatible target listbox and an Edges list; precedents: IBM App Connect Toolkit dialog, Foblex f-flow v19, Blender Make Links (J). Add 'View as table' for viewport analyses (WCAG 1.1.1).

flags.claim: Crameri original maps have no stated licence (UNVERIFIED flag in round 0).
flags.detail: The Zenodo record for Scientific colour maps v8.0.1 (5 Oct 2023, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.8409685) states the MIT License. Source: zenodo.org/records/8409685, opened 21 Oct 2026. The zip contents (66.9 MB) were not listed.

flags.claim: Linked cameras in the Compare view are an unsourced team assumption.
flags.detail: Autodesk's Forma quick-start guide (regional mirror www-pt.autodesk.com, opened 21 Oct 2026) describes Compare for up to six proposals or analysis results, zoom and pan updating all open scenes, and Inspect showing point details in every analysis. The autodesk.com tutorial page itself returned 403.
flags.correction: Cite Forma as precedent for linked cameras and linked point inspection. Whether linking can be switched off is not documented in pages read, so keep an off switch as our own design choice.

flags.claim: Style Dictionary activity and DTCG support are unknown; DTCG 2025.10 can be adopted through it.
flags.detail: npm shows style-dictionary 5.7.0 released 16 Oct 2026 (Apache-2.0). styledictionary.com/info/dtcg says DTCG is first-class since v4 and that full 2025.10 support is still in progress (planned for v5). Read 21 Oct 2026.
flags.correction: The project is active. Author tokens in the DTCG subset v5 supports and note the 2025.10 gaps; for 13 Nov keep plain CSS variables.

flags.claim: We can start from the React Flow UI Workflow Editor template (assumed free to adopt).
flags.detail: reactflow.dev/ui/templates/workflow-editor and /ai-workflow-editor both state 'This is a Pro example'; reactflow.dev/pro lists Starter at $169 per month with Pro examples and templates. The templates use Next.js, ELKjs, Zustand. No page states a licence for the free components; their registry JSON has no licence header. Opened 21 Oct 2026. In r2 the undo/redo example was also found to be a Pro example under the xyflow Pro License.
flags.correction: Do not plan on the templates or the Pro undo/redo example. Build custom nodes on MIT @xyflow/react; treat individual registry components as references until xyflow confirms their licence.

flags.claim: Mark et al. (CHI 2008) cannot be read, so the cost of interrupted work is unverified; interruption was implied to cost time.
flags.detail: The open PDF (author-hosted at ics.uci.edu) was read on 21 Oct 2026. 48 participants did a lab email task and were interrupted by phone or instant message about every two minutes. Interrupted tasks were completed in less time with no difference in quality; the price was more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort; interruption context made no difference; openness to experience and need for personal structure predicted disruption cost.
flags.correction: Cite it as 'faster but more stressed', not as a time cost. Use it to justify protecting edit sessions and deferring non-critical notices, paired with Iqbal and Bailey (CHI 2008, 16 users), where notifications deferred to breakpoints caused less frustration than immediate delivery.

flags.claim: The Cognitive Dimensions tutorial is a binary PDF that could not be read.
flags.detail: The text extracts normally (pdftotext, 21 Oct 2026): Green and Blackwell, Cognitive Dimensions of Information Artefacts: a tutorial, v1.2, October 1998, 75 pages. It lists 14 dimensions (abstraction, hidden dependencies, premature commitment, secondary notation, viscosity, visibility and juxtaposability, closeness of mapping, consistency, diffuseness, error-proneness, hard mental operations, progressive evaluation, provisionality, role-expressiveness) and rates them per activity type.
flags.correction: Apply the framework to the node-canvas contract (weekly walkthrough). The tutorial rates hidden dependencies harmful for modification and exploration. Green and Petre 1996 (J. Visual Languages and Computing 7:131-174) applied it to LabVIEW and Prograph, read here only via a review summary.

flags.claim: In React Flow, the Delete key removes selected edges and nodes by default.
flags.detail: The API reference (read 21 Oct 2026) gives deleteKeyCode the default 'Backspace' (array allowed). The accessibility page's default ARIA text tells users to press delete, which does not match. panActivationKeyCode defaults to Space, which also selects a focused node; zoomOnDoubleClick defaults to true.
flags.correction: Set deleteKeyCode to ['Delete','Backspace'], zoomOnDoubleClick to false (canvas double-click opens search) and panActivationKeyCode to null, and publish one shortcut map. Test it in the keyboard pass.

flags.claim: Microsoft's HAX Toolkit guidelines are unreadable (a poster image), so the AI-UX rules cite no specific guideline.
flags.detail: The 18 guidelines are in text in Amershi et al., CHI 2019 (PDF read with pdftotext) and on Microsoft's research blog, 21 Oct 2026: G1 Make clear what the system can do; G2 how well; G3 Time services based on context; G9 Support efficient correction; G11 Make clear why the system did what it did; G15 Encourage granular feedback; G16 Convey the consequences of user actions; G17 Provide global controls; G18 Notify users about changes.
flags.correction: Cite the CHI 2019 paper and map AI rules to numbered guidelines (principle 15).

flags.claim: Gamification evidence for learning is mixed, as a Wikipedia article summarised.
flags.detail: Sailer and Homner, Educational Psychology Review 32:77-112 (online 2019), abstract read via Semantic Scholar's API on 21 Oct 2026: significant small positive effects on cognitive (g=.49, k=19, N=1686), motivational (g=.36, k=16, N=2246) and behavioural outcomes (g=.25, k=9, N=951); cognitive effects stable in rigorous studies, others less stable; game fiction and competition combined with collaboration moderated behavioural effects. Classroom studies.
flags.correction: Cite the meta-analysis, not Wikipedia. The ban on streaks, points and leaderboards is a values decision for a professional tool, not an evidence finding; learning-supportive feedback (what-changed diffs, shortcut hints, attribution credit) is allowed.

flags.claim: Numeric UI thresholds in our rules are unsourced: seven Essentials per module, 3 significant figures, 200-node warning, six compared options (compact above four), status chips capped at five or six per screen, 12-column board grid, 14 pt body and 10 pt floors, 24 px ports beyond WCAG, cost classes (live under 100 ms, interactive under 1 s, batch longer), 300 ms debounce, 150 dpi warning, pairs under dE76 20 never rely on hue alone.
flags.detail: NN/g supports two disclosure levels, about five comparison items and the 0.1/1/10 s response limits (for acknowledging actions, not results); Forma shows six compared results; Carbon only cautions about five or six indicators; type sizes are scaled from a scientific-poster guide. Mark all as editable team assumptions in the tool.

flags.claim: Starting colour tokens for Sourced, Team assumption, FALSE ASSUMPTION and Failed, and the three-channel palette.
flags.detail: Hex values were chosen by us; contrast computed 21 Oct 2026 (at least 5.43:1 on white, #F4F5F7, #16181C and #22252B; failed 5.5:1 or more). Colour-vision simulation (Machado 2009, severity 1.0, CIELAB dE76) was run by us: Sourced versus FALSE 32 (protan, light) and 17 (protan, dark); the first-draft failed red against ochre 2.2 (deutan). Not tested with people or in the viewport.

flags.claim: Base UI is the right shadcn base for our canvas, palette and popovers.
flags.detail: Chosen because it is shadcn's default and docs follow it. No side-by-side test with React Flow overlays and port popovers was run; Radix remains a '-b radix' fallback and shadcn offers a migration skill.

flags.detail: Instruments chosen by us from sources read in r2 (Mark et al. used a modified NASA-TLX; MeasuringU describes UMUX-Lite). Five participants give descriptive trends only.

flags.detail: The primary chapter (Nakamura and Csikszentmihalyi, Handbook of Positive Psychology) is paywalled and was not opened; the earlier Wikipedia citation was dropped. The Flow-Kurzskala documentation (Rheinberg, Vollmeyer, Engeser; 16 items in three factors, CC BY-SA 4.0 documentation) was opened, but the instrument's own terms and the 10-item Flow Short Scale versions were not. Treat 'flow' as an instrument score to be measured, not a proven design cause.

flags.detail: Hart's 2006 NASA-TLX paper fetch failed; Mark et al. (opened) used a modified NASA-TLX with a stress item on the 20-point scale. UMUX-Lite was read through MeasuringU's summary (two items; r about .83 with SUS; 7-point original, 5-point adaptation less tested), not the 2013 paper.

flags.claim: Lab findings on interruptions generalise to design-tool use.
flags.detail: Mark et al. used an email task; Iqbal and Bailey used diagram editing and programming with 16 users, and for programming the policy differences were not significant. Neither studied a 3D analysis tool. Use as rationale for rules, then test in our sessions.

flags.detail: Our reading of the Understanding page (read 21 Oct 2026): a loading animation can be essential only when users cannot interact, and users can interact during runs. No accessibility audit or assistive-technology test of the canvas has been run.

flags.detail: Read from READMEs and docs only; nothing was run. Yjs docs do not explicitly say remote updates are excluded from undo (they describe origin scoping). zundo README snippets were reported to contain errors by the fetch summary and were not checked.

Annotated benchmark screenshots (Figma, Linear, Speckle, Forma first, with copy and avoid callouts) were not produced; the team should capture them. The Spline editor and the Rerun UI were not analysed.
Autodesk Forma: autodesk.com tutorials return 403; legends, colour scales, units, uncertainty display and whether camera linking toggles are not documented in pages read; no trial run.
Blender node editor conventions (socket inspection, Viewer node, node timings): manual pages too large to read; only Make Links (J) and Mute Links were confirmed.

Impeccable engine binary host and telemetry endpoint not named in the README and not inspected.

Spline editor UX and licence: only the Community Platform docs opened; interface tour not read.
tldraw hobby-licence terms and any educational or open-source exemption: not fetched.
Licences not stated or not checked: React Flow UI components, DTCG, deceptive.design content, Crameri JavaScript packaging (zip contents), W3C document licence, ACM and Microsoft PDF reuse terms.
